newsitem.title: UK: FOCUS-Markka joins ERM without fuss, shares mixed.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS-Markka joins ERM without fuss, shares mixed.

text.p: The Finnish markka made a solid debut in the European Union's currency grid on Monday, while major European stock markets consolidated recent gains at the start of a new week.

In the latest step on the path towards a single EU currency, Finland agreed at the weekend to put the markka into the Exchange Rate Mechanism (ERM), which limits the fluctuations of a majority of current EU currencies against each other.
One of the Maastricht treaty's criteria for membership of European Economic and Monetary Union (EMU) in 1999 is at least two years of membership of the ERM.
The markka traded around 2.9890 to the German mark in morning trading, little changed from Friday's Helsinki close and stronger than its ERM central rate of 3.04.
But its widely signalled entry into the mechanism unsettled forestry stocks in Helsinki, although financial analysts said its rate should not put pressure on exporters.
"From the point of view of fundamentals and competitiveness, this level was quite OK," said Postipankki chief economist Ari Aaltonen.
With European currency news taking the spotlight, the dollar held its ground and currency dealers said it could receive support from fallout from the Finnish move.

"To the extent that Finland's move underlines the EMU process, then it should keep the mark under pressure and the dollar supported," said Joe Prendergast, foreign exchange strategist at Merrill Lynch in London.

But he added that the U.S. currency seemed to lack the fuel for a strong push higher. Traders said many U.S. dealers could be missing for the Columbus Day holiday on Monday, limiting trading activity in currencies.

The pound, meanwhile, hit 2.4192 marks in early trade, its highest since January 1995, and held much of its gains after news of a slightly higher-than expected 0.4 percent rise in British output prices last month.

European bourses, like Wall Street, had been in buoyant mood on Friday, rising on figures which suggested that inflation in the United States, the world's biggest economy, was being kept in check. But they paused for breath on Monday.

Higher futures and strength in the pound helped the London stock market, Europe's biggest, reverse early losses and edge higher in subdued morning business as analysts concluded the latest British data showed little sign of inflationary pressure.
Dealers said sentiment was also boosted by a Merrill Lynch fund managers survey which said institutional investors were growing more optimistic about the British stock market.
But political jitters ahead of an election due by May are still a key background concern. "There's still the worry that this government cannot last the full term," one trader said.
French stocks were lower in thin trading, amid nervousness ahead of a public sector strike on Thursday, but the Frankfurt bourse made moderate gains.

Austrian markets shrugged off a surge in far-right support in European Parliament elections which analysts said was a one-off protest against tough budget cuts. The Vienna bourse was steady in midday trading.
Wall Street will open as usual on Monday although U.S. bond markets will stay shut for the Columbus Day holiday. No major U.S. economic statistics are scheduled for release.
CURRENCIES AT 1130 GMT
The dollar was quoted around 1.5310 marks and 111.65 yen, compared with 1.5307 and 111.67 in late European business on Friday.
STOCK MARKETS AT 1130 GMT
The Financial Times-Stock Exchange index of 100 leading British shares was up 6.9 points at 4,035.0 after earlier losing around 11 points.
In Paris, the CAC-40 share index was down 9.77 at 2,137.35.
The 30-share DAX index in Frankfurt was up 9.09 at 2,695.12.
PRECIOUS METALS
Gold was fixed at $381.05 an ounce in the morning and later traded around $381.15, compared with Friday's London close of $381.35 and afternoon fix of $380.75. Silver edged up to $5.04 from $5.02.
